items.name: part1
items.direction: Narrate this as a popular geography YouTube channel's long-form explainer: a dive from the ocean surface to the deepest point on Earth. The Narrator is a deep, warm, confident storyteller: curious and brisk but never rushed, with natural emphasis, building intrigue as the dive gets deeper and darker, a short comic pause before each punchline, real awe at the big reveals, and quiet seriousness on the lines about people who died. Chars voices funny cartoon sea creatures: short and punchy. Read numbers naturally.
lines: A strong swimmer can dive about 10 metres. With scuba gear, about 40.
The deepest scuba dive ever made went down 332 metres. That's almost two Statues of Unity, stacked.
Sounds deep? It's not even 5 percent of the way down.
Today we jump into the Indian Ocean, sink all the way to the bottom... and then go deeper still.
By 30 metres, your blood looks green. Near the Titanic, a sub was crushed in a split second. And at the very bottom, one man found a fish scientists think is a brand-new species.
The top 200 metres is the sunlight zone. Tiny drifting plants up here make about half the oxygen on Earth. So every other breath you take... thank the ocean.
This is also where you'd meet the biggest fish in the sea. The whale shark. As long as a bus.
Biggest fish in the ocean. And I eat... plankton. Tiny, tiny plankton.
But the light fades fast. Red goes first. By 30 metres, a cut on your hand would bleed dark green.
And every 10 metres down, the sea piles another full sky's worth of air pressure on top of you.
At 182 metres, the Statue of Unity would vanish completely underwater.
At 200 metres, less than 1 percent of the sunlight is left. Welcome to the twilight zone.
Here the water already presses about 20 kilos onto every fingertip. Like balancing a full water jar on each finger.
At 253 metres: the deepest anyone has ever gone on a single breath. Herbert Nitsch, 2012. Coming back up, decompression sickness left him with several strokes.
And Ahmed Gabr's scuba record at 332 metres? Going down took 12 minutes. Coming back up safely took almost 15 hours.
An emperor penguin has been recorded diving 564 metres. That's deeper than a blue whale usually goes.
And at 828 metres, the tallest building on Earth, the Burj Khalifa, would disappear without a trace.
Every single night, something huge happens here. Trillions of animals swim up toward the surface to feed... then sink back down before sunrise.
It's the biggest migration on the planet, by sheer numbers. In World War Two, sonar operators mistook it for the seafloor... a seafloor that moved.
Up every night, down every morning. Worst commute on Earth.

items.name: part2
items.direction: Narrate this as a popular geography YouTube channel's long-form explainer: a dive from the ocean surface to the deepest point on Earth. lines: By 1,000 metres, the sunlight is gone. Completely. Welcome to the midnight zone.
Now every fingertip carries about 100 kilos. Two 50-kilo sacks of rice. On each finger.
Down here, sperm whales hunt giant squid in total darkness. Some whales come back up covered in sucker scars.
So down here, animals make their own light. In one big survey off California, about three quarters of deep-sea animals could glow.
Like the anglerfish. She dangles a glowing lure in front of her mouth... and waits.
Free light! Come closer... a little closer...
In some species, the male is tiny. He bites onto her body, fuses with her, and stays there for life.
At about 2,500 metres, right here in the Indian Ocean, lies the Tilawa, a passenger ship that sailed from Bombay in 1942.
A submarine torpedoed it. 280 people died. Then, in 2017, a salvage team pulled more than 2,000 silver bars back up from the wreck.
Keep sinking. At 3,800 metres you'd pass the depth of the Titanic. Though she lies in another ocean.
In 2023, a small sub called Titan was heading down to that wreck. At around 3,300 metres its hull failed, and the pressure crushed it in a split second. All five people aboard died instantly.
By the Titanic's depth, every fingertip carries about 390 kilos. An entire auto-rickshaw.
At around 4,000 metres, the open water ends... and we reach the abyss. Cold, silent mud. The deep seafloor covers more than half of our planet.
No plants can grow here. Almost everything lives on marine snow: tiny flakes of dead stuff that can take weeks to drift down.
So some animals just wait. The tripod fish stands on three long fins and lets dinner drift into its mouth.
I've been standing here since Tuesday. Totally worth it.
The floor is scattered with metal lumps the size of potatoes. India holds a licence to explore 75,000 square kilometres of them, right here in the Indian Ocean.
At 6,000 metres, the hadal zone begins. Named after Hades, god of the underworld. This is how deep India's own sub, Matsya 6000, is designed to reach.
But the Indian Ocean goes deeper. Into a giant crack south of Indonesia: the Java Trench, where one plate dives under another.
In 2004, an earthquake off Sumatra, on this same trench system, sent tsunamis all the way to India's coast.

lines: Until finally... we hit the bottom. The deepest point in the Indian Ocean. 7,192 metres down.
Every fingertip now carries about 740 kilos. A whole small car.
The first person only got here in 2019: Victor Vescovo, alone in his sub. And through his window, he spotted a snailfish scientists think is a new species.
But this isn't the bottom of the world. Stand Mount Everest here, and its peak would still poke out of the water.
For the deepest place on Earth, we have to cross to the Pacific... and fall another 3.7 kilometres.
The Mariana Trench. Its deepest spot, Challenger Deep, is almost 11 kilometres down.
That's the height planes cruise at. Next time you look out of a plane window, imagine falling that far... under water.
Now flip Everest upside down and drop it in. Its tip still wouldn't touch the bottom. There'd be two kilometres of water to spare.
Every fingertip here carries more than a tonne. A family sedan, on each finger.
The first two people came down here in 1960. On the way, they heard a loud crack. A window had split. They kept going anyway... and stayed 20 minutes.
And life goes almost all the way down. The deepest fish ever filmed was a snailfish at 8,336 metres, off Japan. Below that, shrimp-like creatures carry on to the very bottom.
So how much of the seafloor have we mapped in detail? Less than a third. We have sharper maps of the Moon than of the bottom of our own ocean.
So next time you look at the sea, remember. The shiny blue part is just the lid.
Under it is a world 11 kilometres deep... and almost all of it, no one has ever seen.
This is Bhoogol. Follow for the next dive.
